extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants / patent practitioners (attorneys, agents, inventors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and weighing objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness during patent examination, including commercial success, unexpected results, long-felt need, copying, expert skepticism, and affidavit/declaration requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants have burden of explaining proffered data
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A]ppellants have the burden of explaining the data in any declaration they proffer as evidence of non-obviousness." Ex parte Ishizaka, 24 USPQ2d 1621, 1624 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must provide explanations for any data submitted to support nonobviousness; unexplained data carries less weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected properties may be in the form of a direct or indirect comparison of the claimed invention with the closest prior art which is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative testing (direct or indirect) against the closest prior art to rebut prima facie obviousness. See In re Boesch, In re Blondel, In re Fouche and related MPEP sections for examples where indirect comparative testing was sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of an intermediate via contributing cause and nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product 'when one of ordinary skill in the art would reasonably ascribe to a claimed intermediate the 'contributing cause' for such an unexpectedly superior activity or property.' In re Magerlein, 602 F.2d 366, 373.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must identify the cause of the unexpectedly superior activity in the end product and establish a nexus between that cause and the claimed intermediate; mere correlation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing evidence of expected and unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results must be weighed against evidence supporting a prima facie case of obviousness in making a final determination of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both expected beneficial results (which favor obviousness) and unexpected results (which favor nonobviousness); assess relative significance (see In re May and MPEP § 716.01(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected properties insufficient if not significant relative to expected properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the unexpected properties of a claimed invention are not shown to have a significance equal to or greater than the expected properties, the unexpected properties may not be sufficient to rebut evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the magnitude and practical significance of unexpected properties to expected improvements; if expected improvements are more significant, unexpected properties may fail to rebut obviousness (In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness of a claimed invention, just as unexpected results are evidence of unobviousness thereof." In re Gershon, 372 F.2d 535.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a beneficial result was predictable from the prior art, that fact weighs in favor of obviousness; examiner should cite prior teachings showing the result would have been expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The "objective evidence of non-obviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support." In re Clemens, 622 F.2d 1029.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that unexpected results occur across the entire claimed range; testing limited to narrower conditions may be insufficient to support broad claims (examples: In re Clemens, In re Peterson, In re Grasselli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness of a genus or claimed range may be supported by species/narrow-range data where trend permits
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonobviousness of a broader claimed range can be supported by evidence based on unexpected results from testing a narrower range if one of ordinary skill would be able to determine a trend in the exemplified data allowing reasonable extension of probative value. In re Kollman, 595 F.2d 48.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient exemplified species/range data showing trends that justify extrapolation to the broader claimed range; isolated or inconsistent species data may fail (In re Lindner, Kollman examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range. In re Hill, 284 F.2d 955.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comparative data that demonstrates boundaries or critical points of the claimed range; comparisons only within the range without outside data are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration must compare claimed subject matter with the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness. In re Burckel, 592 F.2d 1175.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the closest single prior art reference (compare claim limitations and relative importance), explain deviations from references, and provide evaluative comparisons; unexplained deviations should be noted and evaluated (In re Merchant, Finley, Armstrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may compare the claimed invention with prior art closer than that applied by the examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may compare the claimed invention with prior art that is more closely related to the invention than the prior art relied upon by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to closer art can be favorable to applicant if they show unexpected properties relative to closer analogs (In re Holladay; Ex parte Humber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons when two equally close prior art references exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing unexpected results over one of two equally close prior art references will not rebut prima facie obviousness unless the teachings of the prior art references are sufficiently similar that testing of one would provide the same information as to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applicant tests less than all cited compounds, tests must be sufficient to permit conclusions about relative effectiveness across the closest prior art; see In re Johnson and In re Payne for standards and emphasis on sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention may only be compared to subject matter existing in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Although evidence must compare the claimed invention with the closest prior art, applicant is not required to compare with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require hypothetical or post-combination polymers/structures that are not actually disclosed in the prior art (In re Geiger; In re Chapman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages disclosed or inherent may be considered even if not in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; the totality of the record must be considered. In re Chu, 66 F.3d 292.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant's proffered advantages (even if first raised during prosecution) can be probative if supported by evidence; specification need not disclose proportions or values as critical to present evidence of criticality (Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration or affidavit form requirement and role of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reason for requiring evidence in declaration or affidavit form is to obtain the assurances that any statements or representations made are correct..." Ex parte Gray, 10 USPQ2d 1922.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use declarations/affidavits to obtain sworn assurance; publications may be considered as probative evidence but do not substitute for the statutory assurances of affidavits/declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success requires nexus to claimed invention; applicant bears burden
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and evidence of commercial success. In re Huang, 100 F.3d 135.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide hard evidence linking sales/market performance to claimed features; the PTO will rely on applicant to supply such evidence in ex parte prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness including commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims. Evidence limited to a narrower product/feature set not recited in the broad claims is insufficient. In re Tiffin, 448 F.2d 791.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the commercial success is due to features encompassed by the claims, not unclaimed features; dependent-claim-only features cannot support broad independent claims (Joy Technologies; Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: When claimed invention not coextensive with commercial product, show legal relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: If the commercially successful product or process is not coextensive with the claimed invention, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product or process. Demaco Corp. v. F. Von Langsdorff Licensing Ltd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the typical commercial point(s) within the claimed ranges approximate operation throughout the claimed ranges or otherwise link the commercial success to claimed features (In re Hollingsworth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not marketing or unrelated factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success alleged must be directly derived from the invention claimed... and not the result of heavy promotion or advertising, brand loyalty, or other business events extraneous to the merits of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence that purchasers chose the product for the patented features; conclusory statements or inventor opinions are insufficient (In re Mageli; In re Huang; Pentec; Fielder; EWP; Hybritech examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: To be pertinent, the commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success due to later modifications by others is not probative. In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link commercial performance to disclosed/inherent advantages of the claimed invention rather than to external improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: In design cases, establishing nexus for commercial success is especially difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design to be of probative value, and not to brand name recognition, improved performance, or some other factor. Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide direct evidence attributing sales or market acceptance specifically to the claimed design features, not to brand or unrelated attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures do not show commercial success absent evidence as to market share, the time period during which the product was sold, or what sales would normally be expected in the market. Cable Electric Products, Inc. v. Genmark, Inc.; Ex parte Standish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include market-share data, relevant timeframes, and baseline expectations to contextualize gross sales numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need and failure of others: requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must satisfy a long-felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not solved by others. Establishing this requires objective evidence that an art-recognized problem existed for a long period without solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the problem was recognized by those of ordinary skill, persisted over time, and was not previously solved; consider licensing affidavits, industry recognition, and prior unsuccessful efforts (In re Gershon; Orthopedic Equipment; Newell; Cavanagh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need is measured from the date a problem is identified and efforts are made
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-felt need is analyzed as of the date the problem is identified and articulated, and there is evidence of efforts to solve it, not as of the date of the most pertinent prior art references. Texas Instruments Inc. v. Int’l Trade Comm’n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor the analysis to when the need was recognized and when attempts to solve it occurred; later recognition is less probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors may explain failure of others (e.g., lack of interest) and must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure to solve a long-felt need may be due to factors such as lack of interest or lack of appreciation of an invention’s potential or marketability rather than want of technical know-how. Scully Signal Co. v. Electronics Corp. of America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate alternative explanations for why others did not solve the problem; absence of attempts does not automatically imply nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts is strong evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Expressions of disbelief by experts constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness." Environmental Designs, Ltd. v. Union Oil Co. of Cal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony showing expert skepticism (especially pre-invention) and long research efforts preceding the invention can weigh substantially in favor of nonobviousness (In re Dow; Burlington).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying as secondary evidence: more than mere fact required
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors are copying the invention can be presented, but more than mere copying is needed; copying may be attributable to other factors and is persuasive only where competitors expended effort and failed before copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show attempted independent development and failure followed by copying, and that copies are substantially identical and motivated by the invention's merits (Cable Electric; Dow Chem.; Pentec; Panduit examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of operability of references; affidavits attacking operability must rebut by preponderance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent is presumed valid, including a presumption of operability. Affidavits or declarations attacking the operability of a patent cited as a reference must rebut the presumption by a preponderance of the evidence. In re Sasse, 629 F.2d 675.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide convincing, probative evidence when alleging a prior-art reference is inoperative; mere difficulty operating within a disclosure or failure by disinterested experimenters carries limited weight (In re Weber; Michalek; Reid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability claims limited to asserted features; reference remains effective for operative features
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the affidavit asserts inoperability in features of the reference which are not relied upon, the reference is still effective as to other operative features. In re Shepherd, 172 F.2d 560.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish which features of a reference are alleged inoperative; inability to show inoperability for relied-on features leaves the reference effective for obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's declaration of nonintent to practice a reference is immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent teaches or suggests the claimed invention, an affidavit or declaration by the patentee that he or she did not intend the disclosed invention to be used as claimed by applicant is immaterial. In re Pio, 217 F.2d 956.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the disclosure itself rather than the patentee's asserted intent; typographical errors or demonstrable mistakes in the reference may be exceptional (In re Yale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and operability of applicant’s disclosure (reference to MPEP §2107 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: See MPEP § 2107.02 for guidance on when it is proper to require evidence of utility or operativeness, and how to evaluate any evidence submitted to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP §2107–§2107.03 when examining utility/operability issues; require appropriate evidence when utility is in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (reference to MPEP §2164 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: See MPEP § 2164 - § 2164.08(c) for guidance in determining whether the specification provides an enabling disclosure in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the enablement guidance in MPEP §2164 when assessing whether the specification teaches how to make and use the claimed invention over the full scope claimed.
